newsitem.title: GERMANY: Prodi, before Kohl meeting, pledges iron discipline.
newsitem.headline: Prodi, before Kohl meeting, pledges iron discipline.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi insisted in German newspaper interviews published on Friday, hours before he was due to meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl, that Italy would belong to Europe's single currency despite German doubts.

He singled out Germany's commercial banks, its central bank, the Bundesbank, and the British press as the main forces in a campaign against Italian membership of the planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Prodi, who was due to arrive in Bonn at around 1000 GMT for talks with Kohl, told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily that Italy would use "iron discipline" to meet the Maastricht criteria for EMU, scheduled to begin in 1999.

Italian membership of EMU has leapt to the top of the European political agenda following reports that EU officials and central bankers were drafting a plan to defer Rome's entry, partly to assuage German fears of a soft single currency.
"The process of restructuring and stabilising in Italy is continuing," Prodi said. "Italy in the past did not fulfil any of the Maastricht criteria."

"In contrast to that, we now fulfil several of them. For example our inflation rate is 2.5 percent to 2.6 percent. I do not see any difference between Italy and Germany in the fight against inflation."
Now, it was important to use "iron discipline" to reduce the budget deficit to below three percent of gross domestic product, as the Maastricht Treaty demands.
"We know that we'll be outside the currency union if we're over three percent," Prodi said.
He dismissed the suggestion that Italy was manipulating its accounting to qualify, saying every change in bookkeeping practices was examined in advance by European institutions.
He also said Italy could not afford to plead for a delay in the start of the currency union. "We can't even allow ourselves even the thought of a postponement. We just have to run."

Prodi said if Italy failed to qualify for EMU, the country's financial markets could come under a wave of speculative attack that would lead to devaluation and rising inflation. "We would become a centre of unrest in Europe," he predicted.

In a separate interview with the Handelsblatt business daily, Prodi said he was certain that Italy would be among the first countries to join EMU. "Italy will belong to the currency union from the start," he said.
